source_text: Numquam quippe diceret: Si mortui non resurgunt, nec Christus resurrexit; cui poterat referri: Sed Christus, quoniam de Virgine natus est, peculiariter resurrexit; homines autem, quia nati sunt de commixtione diabolica, non resurgunt. Verum ille protinus referret: Et quae fuit resurgendi vanitas, si nec spei nostrae nec magisterio parabatur? Quae enim esset ratio docendi, quae gravitas exempli, si natura in nobis dissimilis, et spe conregnandi, et vi careret imitandi? Procul igitur, et nimis procul fides Apostoli ab hac opinione consistit. Eodem plenus spiritu, quo etiam Petrus, scit Christum pro nobis ob hoc mortuum, ut nobis donaret exemplum, ut sequeremur vestigia eius [n207] . Et quia causam tanti mysterii, sacrificium novit et exemplum fuisse, pronuntiare non dubitat, immo diligenter inculcat, quia non accesserit homo Christus aliquo, a quo quisquam nostrum naturae suae praeiudiciis arceatur. Si - inquit - resurrectio non est mortuorum, neque Christus resurrexit. Si autem Christus ex mortuis resurrexit, quomodo dicunt quidam in vobis quia resurrectio mortuorum non est? Id est, si confitemini eiusdem illum secundum hominem, cuius nos, fuisse naturae, qua ratione vel in illo factam resurrectionem, vel in reliquis non futuram putatis? Praemissis conditionibus, implet ex omni parte sententiam: Nunc autem - inquit - Christus resurrexit ex mortuis; erit ergo resurrectio mortuorum.
pass_a_gloss: For he would never have said: If the dead do not rise, neither did Christ rise; to whom it could be reported: But Christ, because he was born from a Virgin, rose peculiarly; but humans, because they were born from a diabolical mingling, do not rise. But he would immediately report: And what was the vanity of rising, if it was being prepared neither for our hope nor for teaching? For what would be the reason of teaching, what the gravity of an example, if a nature dissimilar in us would lack both a hope of co-reigning and a force of imitating? Far therefore, and too far, the Apostle's faith stands from this opinion. Full of the same spirit, by which even Peter, he knows that Christ died for us on account of this, that he might give us an example, that we might follow his footsteps. And because he knows the cause of so great a mystery was a sacrifice and an example, he does not doubt to pronounce, nay he diligently impresses, that the human Christ did not accede by something, from which anyone of us is kept off by the prior judgments of his nature. If, he says, there is not a resurrection of the dead, neither did Christ rise. But if Christ rose from the dead, how do certain people say among you that there is not a resurrection of the dead? That is, if you confess that he according to the human was of the same nature of which we, by what reason do you think either a resurrection made in him, or not future in the rest? The conditions having been sent ahead, he fills the sentence from every part: But now, he says, Christ rose from the dead; there will therefore be a resurrection of the dead.

pass_b_english: He would never say, ‘If the dead do not rise, Christ has not risen either,’ if someone could reply: But Christ rose exceptionally because he was born from a virgin; humans do not rise because they were born from a diabolical union. He would immediately answer: Then what was the empty point of rising, if it served neither our hope nor our instruction? What reasonable teaching or weighty example could there be if a nature unlike ours left us without both the hope of reigning with him and the power to imitate him?

The apostle’s faith stands far, very far from this opinion. Filled with the same Spirit as Peter, he knows Christ died for us to give us an example, so that we might follow his footsteps (1 Peter 2:21). Knowing that sacrifice and example were the purpose of so great a mystery, he does not hesitate to pronounce—indeed, carefully stresses—that Christ the human has reached no place from which any of us is excluded by our nature’s condition.

‘If there is no resurrection of the dead,’ he says, ‘Christ has not risen either. But if Christ has risen from the dead, how do some among you say there is no resurrection of the dead?’ (1 Corinthians 15:12–13). That is: If you acknowledge him, as human, to have possessed the same nature as ours, on what grounds do you either think resurrection occurred in him or will not occur in the rest? Having set out the conditions, he completes the judgment on every side: ‘But now Christ has risen from the dead’ (1 Corinthians 15:20); therefore there will be resurrection of the dead.
